title: DNA, replication and biotechnology
summary: The structure of DNA, how it is copied, mutations and biotechnology
cards.0.p: The building block of DNA is called a nucleotide. A nucleotide is made of a phosphate, a deoxyribose sugar and a base. The bases are A, G, T and C. The double-ringed A and G are called purines, and the single-ringed T and C are called pyrimidines.
cards.0.key: The bases are named adenine, guanine, thymine and cytosine. The base attaches to the sugar's 1' carbon, and the phosphate to its 5' carbon.
cards.1.p: Starting from Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photo, Watson and Crick built the double helix model in 1953. DNA looks like a twisted ladder. The sides of the ladder are sugar-phosphate chains, and the rungs are base pairs.
cards.1.key: Nucleotides in the same strand are joined by phosphodiester bonds. In linear double-stranded DNA, the number of phosphodiester bonds is the number of nucleotides minus 2.
cards.1.once.soru: If we compare the double helix to a twisted ladder, what do the rungs stand for?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: The paired bases are the rungs that join the two strands.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: The sugar-phosphate chains are the sides of the ladder.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: The rungs are made of bases, not proteins.
cards.2.p: Paired bases hold on to each other with hydrogen bonds. There are two hydrogen bonds between A and T, and three between G and C. The two strands are antiparallel. One runs 5'→3', and the other runs 3'→5'.
cards.2.key: A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, so the width of the helix stays the same. The weak bonds let the strands come apart easily. DNA with a high G–C share is harder to separate.
cards.3.p: In double-stranded DNA, the number of adenines equals the number of thymines (A = T), and the number of guanines equals the number of cytosines (G = C). For example, if 200 base pairs contain 80 A, then T = 80, and G and C are 120 each.
cards.3.key: That is why A + G = T + C. The number of hydrogen bonds in the example is 2·80 + 3·120 = 520. This rule does not hold for a single strand or for RNA.
cards.3.etk.soru: Change the number of A–T and G–C pairs in a double-stranded DNA.
cards.4.p: In RNA, the sugar is ribose, and uracil (U) takes the place of thymine. RNA is usually single-stranded. mRNA carries information, tRNA brings amino acids and rRNA is part of the ribosome.
cards.4.svg#17: Shared: phosphate and the bases A, G, C
cards.4.key: T is found only in DNA, and U only in RNA. A, G and C are found in both. The details are in the topic Protein synthesis.
cards.4.once.soru: Which base is not found in RNA?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: RNA has uracil (U) in place of thymine.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: A, G and C are found in both DNA and RNA.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: A, G and C are found in both DNA and RNA.
cards.5.p: A section of DNA that carries the information for a protein or an RNA is called a gene. DNA wraps around histone proteins to form chromatin. During division, chromatin packs tightly and is called a chromosome. All the genetic information of an organism is called its genome.
cards.5.svg#7: Genome = all of an organism's genetic information
cards.5.once.soru: What is the difference between chromatin and a chromosome?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Both are the same DNA. During division, chromatin packs tightly and becomes a chromosome.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: The genes are the same. The only thing that changes is how tightly the DNA is packed.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.yazi: One is DNA, the other protein
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Both are DNA wrapped around histones.
cards.6.p: After replication, each new DNA molecule has one old strand and one new strand. This is called semiconservative replication. In 1958, Meselson and Stahl showed this with bacteria they moved from a ¹⁵N medium to a ¹⁴N medium.
cards.6.key: If replication were conservative, the first replication would show two separate bands, one heavy and one light.
cards.7.p: DNA replication happens during interphase. Helicase separates the strands. Primase makes a short RNA primer. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the end of the primer and works only in the 5'→3' direction.
cards.7.key: DNA polymerase cannot start a chain from scratch. Helicase opens, primase starts, polymerase builds and ligase joins the pieces. This process uses energy.
cards.8.p: As the replication fork opens, the leading strand grows continuously. The other strand is built in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, and ligase joins these pieces. This strand is called the lagging strand.
cards.8.key: A single primer is enough for the leading strand. Each Okazaki fragment starts with its own primer, and the primers are later replaced with DNA. Both strands grow in the 5'→3' direction.
cards.8.once.soru: DNA polymerase can build only in the 5'→3' direction. As the fork opens, how are the two strands built?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: The strands are antiparallel. One is built continuously toward the fork, and the other is built backward in pieces.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: The strands are antiparallel, so one has to be built in the direction away from the fork.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: The strand that grows toward the fork can be built continuously.
cards.9.p: A lasting change in DNA is called a mutation. In a gene mutation, the bases change. Sickle-cell anemia is an example. In a chromosome mutation, a part of a chromosome or the number of chromosomes changes. Down syndrome is an example. Mutagens make mutations more likely.
cards.9.key: Bases can be changed, deleted or inserted. UV, X-rays and some chemicals in cigarette smoke are mutagens. A mutation in a germ cell passes to the offspring.
cards.9.once.soru: In Down syndrome, there are three copies of chromosome 21. What kind of mutation is this?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: The chromosome number has changed. There are 47 chromosomes instead of 46.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Here it is not the bases of one gene that changed. A whole extra chromosome is present.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Every lasting change in DNA is a mutation.
cards.10.p: A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at specific places. The insulin gene is joined into a bacterium's plasmid with ligase, forming recombinant DNA. As the bacterium multiplies, it makes human insulin.
cards.10.key: A plasmid is a bacterium's ring-shaped DNA. The restriction enzyme works like scissors, ligase like glue and the plasmid like a carrier (vector).
cards.10.once.soru: Where is most of the human insulin used by people with diabetes made today?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: The human insulin gene is moved into these organisms, and they make the insulin.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Getting insulin from blood would give small amounts and be expensive.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: Insulin comes from genetically modified microbes, not from plants.
cards.11.p: PCR is a method for copying a piece of DNA in a tube, and the number of copies doubles with every cycle. DNA fingerprinting compares regions that are unique to each person. It is used in criminal cases and paternity tests.
cards.11.key: When DNA is heated, the strands separate, primers attach and a heat-resistant DNA polymerase builds the new strand. n cycles give 2ⁿ copies. Identical twins have the same DNA fingerprint.
cards.12.p: In gene therapy, a working gene is carried into cells by a harmless virus to replace a gene that has lost its function. Organisms whose genes have been changed are called GMOs. Cloning means producing organisms that are genetically identical.
cards.12.key: Dolly was the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell.
cards.12.once.soru: What do we call corn that has been given a bacterial gene to make it resistant to insects?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: An organism that has received a gene from another species is called a genetically modified organism.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: A clone is an exact copy of an organism. Here, a new gene has been added.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: A hybrid comes from crossing two varieties, and no gene from another species is moved.
cards.13.p: Stem cells are cells that have not yet specialized, and they can become nerve, muscle or blood cells. They are found in embryos, bone marrow and umbilical cord blood. These technologies also raise bioethical questions.
cards.13.key: Using embryos, keeping genetic information private, the effect of GMOs on nature and human cloning are bioethical questions. Science tells us what can be done. What should be done is an ethical question.
cards.13.once.soru: A leukemia patient gets a bone marrow transplant. Which cells make the new blood cells?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Stem cells in the bone marrow divide and become blood cells.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: Muscle cells are specialized and cannot make blood cells.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: Nerve cells are specialized and are not found in bone marrow.
cards.14.p: A genetic test looks for specific changes in DNA. A carrier test is an example. In genetic counseling, couples are told about the risks, which matters especially when relatives marry. The family makes the decision.
cards.14.svg#11: carrier × carrier: each child has a 1/4 chance of the condition
cards.14.svg#12: Results are private, the decision is the family's
cards.14.key: The newborn heel-prick test looks at substances in the blood, not at DNA. For example, in phenylketonuria it measures excess phenylalanine. Screening for Down syndrome is also done during pregnancy. The results are kept private.
cards.14.once.soru: What is the chance that a child of two carrier parents gets a recessive condition?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: In an Aa × Aa cross, 1/4 of the children are aa.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: 1/2 is the chance that the child is a carrier (Aa).
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: The parents are not affected, but both carry the recessive allele.
cards.15.p:
• A nucleotide is made of a phosphate, deoxyribose and a base. There are 2 hydrogen bonds between A and T, and 3 between G and C.
• In double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C.
• Replication is semiconservative.
• Mutations happen at the gene or chromosome level.
• Biotechnology includes recombinant DNA, PCR, fingerprinting and cloning.
quiz.0.q: A double-stranded DNA of 2,000 nucleotides has 600 adenines. How many hydrogen bonds does this DNA have in total?
quiz.0.e: T = 600, and G and C are (2,000 − 1,200) / 2 = 400 each. The 600 A–T pairs make 2 bonds each, and the 400 G–C pairs make 3 bonds each. The total is 1,200 + 1,200 = 2,400 hydrogen bonds.
quiz.1.q: Put the events on the lagging strand during DNA replication in order.
quiz.1.ogeler.0: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds and separates the strands
quiz.1.ogeler.1: Primase makes a short RNA primer
quiz.1.ogeler.2: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the end of the primer
quiz.1.ogeler.3: The RNA primers are removed and replaced with DNA
quiz.1.e: First, helicase separates the strands. Polymerase cannot start a chain from scratch, so primase makes a primer and polymerase extends it. Then the primers are replaced with DNA, and ligase joins the pieces.
quiz.2.q: Match each biotechnology term with its description.
quiz.2.ciftler.0.1: Cuts DNA at a specific sequence
quiz.2.ciftler.2.1: Copies a piece of DNA in a tube
quiz.2.ciftler.3.1: Compares regions unique to a person
quiz.2.ciftler.4.1: A cell that has not yet specialized
quiz.2.e: A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at specific sequences. A plasmid is a bacterium's small, ring-shaped DNA. PCR copies a piece of DNA in a tube, and fingerprinting compares regions unique to a person. A stem cell is a cell that has not yet specialized.
quiz.3.q: A linear, double-stranded DNA is made of 1,200 nucleotides. How many phosphodiester bonds are there in total in the strands of this DNA?
quiz.3.e: Each strand is made of 600 nucleotides and has 599 phosphodiester bonds. The two strands have 2 · 599 = 1,198 bonds in total. One molecule of water was released as each bond formed.
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Pair the bases, calculate with Chargaff's rule and watch DNA being copied.
A:adimlar.0.metin: DNA has four bases: A, G, T and C. Count their rings and find which ones have two rings.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which two bases have two rings (purines)?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: T and C have one ring. They are pyrimidines.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Adenine and guanine are double-ringed purines. Thymine and cytosine are single-ringed pyrimidines. Uracil in RNA also has one ring.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: A has two rings, but T has one. Count the rings again.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The two strands hold on to each other through hydrogen bonds between their bases. A always pairs with T, and G always pairs with C. The strands are antiparallel. Guess the partner of the top strand.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: This is a copy of the same sequence and does not follow the pairing rule.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: U is found only in RNA. In DNA, T pairs with A.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: T pairs with A, A with T, C with G and G with C. The direction is reversed too, so it runs 3'→5'. There are two hydrogen bonds between A and T, and three between G and C.
A:adimlar.2.metin: An A–T pair has 2 hydrogen bonds, and a G–C pair has 3. Change the number of adenines in this 100-base-pair DNA and make the number of hydrogen bonds 270.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: With 30 adenines, T = 30, and G and C are 70 each. The number of hydrogen bonds is 2·30 + 3·70 = 270. The more G–C pairs there are, the more bonds there are and the harder it is to separate the strands.
A:adimlar.3.metin: When DNA is copied, the two strands separate and each one acts as a template for a new strand. Meselson and Stahl copied DNA containing heavy ¹⁵N twice in a light ¹⁴N medium.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: After the second replication, how many of the 4 DNA molecules contain an old (heavy) strand?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: There are only two old strands, and they do not break apart. So they can end up in only two molecules.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The old strands are not lost. In every replication, they stay inside the new molecules as templates.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The two old strands go into two different molecules. This gives 2 hybrid and 2 light DNA molecules. After the first replication, all molecules are hybrid. Each new molecule has one old and one new strand. This is called semiconservative replication.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Play the replication fork and see which enzyme does what.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: Which enzyme breaks the hydrogen bonds between the two strands and separates them?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Ligase glues pieces together. It does not separate the strands.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: DNA polymerase builds the new strand by adding nucleotides that match the template. The strands are opened before that.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Helicase moves along at the tip of the fork, breaks the hydrogen bonds and opens the two strands.
A:adimlar.5.metin: PCR copies a piece of DNA in a tube. First the DNA is heated and the strands separate, then primers attach and the new strand is built. The number of copies doubles with every cycle. Increase the number of cycles and get at least 1,000 copies.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: 10 cycles give 2¹⁰ = 1,024 copies. That is why a DNA fingerprint can be made from even a single hair root or bloodstain at a crime scene.
A:kapanis.0: A nucleotide is made of a phosphate, a deoxyribose sugar and a base. Purines (A, G) have two rings, and pyrimidines (T, C) have one.
A:kapanis.1: There are two hydrogen bonds between A and T, and three between G and C. The two strands run in opposite directions.
A:kapanis.2: By Chargaff's rule, in double-stranded DNA the number of A equals the number of T, and the number of G equals the number of C.
A:kapanis.3: Replication is semiconservative. Helicase opens the strands, DNA polymerase builds and ligase joins the pieces.
A:kapanis.4: In PCR, each cycle doubles the number of copies. n cycles give 2ⁿ copies.
